newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euroclear urges common EMU bond conversion rules.
newsitem.headline: Euroclear urges common EMU bond conversion rules.

text.p: Euroclear, the world's largest clearance and settlement system for international securities, on Monday urged financial markets to adopt a common approach to redenominating national debt once a single currency is launched.
Most European Union governments are expected to convert their outstanding national debt into the euro, the new single currency, after economic and monetary union begins on January 1, 1999.

The debt redenomination, coupled with new debt issuance in the euro, is expected to create a deep and common bond market that could eventually rival the U.S. government securities market, market experts say.
But the process of agreeing rules for debt redenomination has been criticised for not proceeding quickly enough and for lacking a sole independent body which could impose a common approach.

"Despite the various calls by financial intermediaries and industry bodies to achieve harmonisation of securities redenomination methods, progress towards harmonisation is unlikely," Euroclear said, outlining a list of potential minimum standards.

Among the various issues which need clarification, it said there should be agreement on the date when securities would be redenominated, the method, rules on rounding and various other technical issues.

"Defining a set of standards which all market players can use will avoid confusion related to possible misinterpretation," said Yves Poullet, vice president at Euroclear Operations Centre in Brussels.

The European Commission, the EU's executive, and the European Monetary Institute, forerunner to a European Central Bank, have been involved in canvassing views from financial markets over the best course of action in debt conversion.
In July, the Commission unveiled a lengthy report outlining a series of recommendations put together from consultations with a large number of banks and financial firms.
So far, only Luxembourg, Belgium and France have officially said they would redenominate their old debt into the euro from the beginning of monetary union in 1999.
Germany, however, has recently said it would most likely redenominate its outstanding debt as well.
The difficulty many financial firms face is the lack of a single EU authority which has power to enforce a common set of practices.
This has increased uncertainty in the run-up to the euro's introduction.
Both the Commission and the EMI argue that they lack legislative authority to impose common rules and want markets to reach agreement on the many complex and important issues such a process involves.
Euroclear also urged that the timing for redenomination of securities should be synchronised between different European and International Centralised Securities Depositaries (CSDs).
"The daily average settlement volumes in the Euroclear System for European government debt securities is today around $135 billion," the group said.
"Taken as a proxy for the wider marketplace, the possible disruption due to redenonimation difficulties could have far-reaching implications." REUTER
